A by-election for the United Kingdom parliamentary constituency of Clacton was held on 13 August 2026, following the resignation of Nigel Farage, its member of Parliament. Farage, who is the leader of Reform UK, had represented Clacton since the 2024 general election. He announced on 7 July 2026 that he would vacate his seat to trigger a by-election and re-contest the constituency; his resignation was accepted the next day. The announcement came amid parliamentary scrutiny of Farage's personal finances, and allegations concerning undeclared gifts and support.

The Labour Party, the Conservative Party, the Liberal Democrats, the Green Party and Restore Britain did not contest the by-election, leaving Count Binface, a novelty candidate, as the main challenger to Farage. Thirty-two other candidates were nominated, with the total of 34 breaking the record – previously set in 2008 – for the most candidates standing in any UK parliamentary election. The list included 18 independent candidates.

Farage was re-elected with 22,239 votes (63.3% of those cast), followed by Binface with 9,455 (26.9%). The other 32 candidates received 3,417 (9.73%) of the vote, ranging from 7 to 492 (1.4%) votes per candidate. 20 candidates received 60 votes (0.17%) or less, including three different candidates from the Official Monster Raving Loony Party.

Background

Clacton

Clacton is a coastal constituency in Essex, in the East of England. It is centred on Clacton-on-Sea and also includes other towns and villages in the Tendring area, including Frinton-on-Sea, Walton-on-the-Naze and Jaywick. According to 2021 census data, its residents are 96% ethnically White, and 44% of its residents belong to social grades A, B and C1.[1] The average gross household income is £33,147, below the average of £42,397 for Great Britain as a whole, and the home-ownership rate is 73%, against 64% nationally.[2] In the 2016 membership referendum, an estimated 73% of those who voted chose to leave the European Union.[3] The constituency is also known for being a target seat for right-wing populist parties;[4] the 2014 Clacton by-election was contested and won by Douglas Carswell, who had resigned as the member of Parliament (MP) for the constituency after defecting from the Conservative Party to the UK Independence Party (UKIP; at the time also led by Nigel Farage). The result made Carswell UKIP's first elected MP.[5]

Investigation into Farage

Farage's declaration that he was standing down followed reports of parliamentary investigations into his financial interests, his relationships with wealthy people, and other matters.[6][7][8] Specifically, the investigations involved: a payment of £5 million from the Thailand-based British businessman and cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne;[6] possible gifts in kind from George Cottrell, a British financier and political activist who was convicted of felony wire fraud in the United States in 2017;[9] allegations of lobbying the Bank of England regarding cryptocurrency;[10] declaration of several properties.[10]

Farage's resignation interrupted the investigation process, though it would resume if he returned to Parliament.[11] Were Farage to be suspended from Parliament for more than 10 sitting days or 14 calendar days, it would trigger a recall petition, which if successful would result in a further by-election.[12] In addition to the parliamentary investigation, on the day of Farage's resignation as an MP it was reported that the £5 million payment from Harborne had also been reported to the United Kingdom's National Crime Agency by bankers under the anti-money laundering suspicious activity report scheme.[13][14] Other donations to Reform UK and other party leaders have also been flagged under the scheme.[15]

Vacation of the seat

On 7 July 2026 Farage announced that he would vacate his seat as MP for Clacton and stand again in the resulting by-election. He gave the investigations into him and his treatment by the press as reasons. Farage denied wrongdoing and said that he wanted voters in Clacton, rather than the press or parliamentary authorities, to decide whether he should continue as their MP.[16][17] On 8 July, Rachel Reeves, the chancellor of the exchequer, formalised his resignation by appointing him to the office of profit post of Steward and Bailiff of the Manor of Northstead to vacate his seat (as outright resignation from the Commons is not possible).[18] While objecting to his motives for resigning, she said "if he wants to spend the summer arguing with a bin, I won't stop him".[19][20] The writ to trigger the by-election was moved on 9 July,[21][22] and the date of 13 August was selected.[23] In the 21st century, there have been four instances where an incumbent MP has resigned and immediately stood in the ensuing by-election: David Davis at the 2008 Haltemprice and Howden by-election,[24] Douglas Carswell at the 2014 Clacton by-election,[25] Mark Reckless at the 2014 Rochester and Strood by-election[26] and Zac Goldsmith at the 2016 Richmond Park by-election.[27] All but Goldsmith retained their seats.

Candidates

The Statement of Persons Nominated was published after nominations closed on 17 July 2026.[23] Thirty-four candidates stood, breaking the record of 26 set at the 2008 Haltemprice and Howden by-election.[28][29] The large number of candidates resulted in the creation of the UK's largest ballot papers, measuring 90 cm (3 ft) in length, which cost four times more to print than regular ballots.[30] Ian Davidson, chief executive of Tendring District Council, told the BBC that the ballots, being longer than some of the tables used to count them on, meant that tables would have to be doubled for sorting ballots into batches before they could be verified and counted.[31]

Declined to stand

Shortly after Farage's announcement, the Labour Party, the Conservative Party, the Green Party, the Liberal Democrats and Restore Britain all stated they would not contest the by-election.[32][33] A Labour spokesperson called the situation "pathetic",[34] while Restore Britain leader Rupert Lowe said his party would not participate in "a Reform-sponsored media circus".[35] Green Party deputy leader Mothin Ali initially said (on 7 July) that the Greens stand in "every election",[36] but the party confirmed later that day that it would not nominate a candidate, describing the by-election as being designed to "serve Nigel Farage's personal political ambitions".[17]

The Conservatives were reported to be targeting the seat in the next UK general election, but the party's leader, Kemi Badenoch, said that they would not stand in "Farage's fake by-election".[35] On 7 August, she wrote an open letter saying her party would participate in any second by-election.[37] The film journalist David Hughes, who stood as Lord Buckethead for the Official Monster Raving Loony Party at the 2019 general election in Uxbridge and South Ruislip, said many people had asked him to stand as Buckethead in Clacton, but that he was finished with the character and endorsed Count Binface instead.[38]

Campaign

Reform UK

Farage denied wrongdoing and described the contest as a "people versus the establishment" by-election.[17] Reform offered to pay for the costs of the by-election, estimated at around £200,000, but the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government stated that this would be illegal since elections are required to solely use public funds.[39][40] In an interview with the Daily Mail, Farage denied accusations that the by-election was a "farce", calling it a "real election with real people". He expressed surprise at the other parties' decision not to field candidates, which he described as "showing contempt" towards the electorate.[41]

The Guardian reported on 9 July that Reform UK called on party activists to shift their focus from the Greater Manchester mayoral by-election on 30 July to support Farage in Clacton. Reform UK responded to the report by stating: "Our campaign plans for the Greater Manchester mayor by-election remain unchanged."[42] On 23 July, while Farage was campaigning in Clacton, a woman heckled Farage, shouting "wanker" as she drove past him, but while doing so crashed into the car in front of her while it was waiting at traffic lights. Farage later said: "That's what you might call instant karma!" in reference to the incident.[43][44]

Count Binface Party

After the major parties declined to contest the election, the perennial novelty candidate Count Binface became the main contender to Farage in early media coverage, with The Independent reporting that Binface had become the focus of an anti-Farage tactical voting campaign.[45] Binface described himself as a "unity candidate".[46] In an interview with BBC Radio 4, Binface conceded that he would "probably not" win the election, but said that his job was "to celebrate and defend the wonders of British democracy".[47] He said his main appeal would be that he is not Farage.[48]

Many mainstream politicians reacted to Binface's candidature with a mixture of amusement and approbation.[49] Badenoch, the Leader of the Opposition, said that if the by-election was a "people versus the establishment" that "Farage might be looking like the establishment and Count Binface maybe the people".[50] Keir Starmer, the prime minister, said he could not endorse Binface due to Labour Party rules.[51] Andy Burnham, who became prime minister the following month, posted a picture of himself shaking hands with Binface at a by-election.[52] He later said that Binface was "carrying the hopes of the nation".[53]

Binface received a surge of support from activists after announcing his candidacy, raising more than £15,000 in donations in a day. He said he hoped to appeal to voters from all sides of the political spectrum and said he could even court the immigrant vote, given he was "the ultimate alien".[51] The green-energy industrialist Dale Vince, who has previously donated to Labour and the Green Party, offered to fund Binface's campaign.[54] Mr. C, former frontman of the psychedelic band the Shamen, re-recorded the band's 1992 number one single "Ebeneezer Goode" with lyrics about Binface, and filmed a music video.[55] Media personality Carol Vorderman urged Clacton's voters to support Binface.[56] Binface's campaign gained global media attention,[57][58] and has inspired a flood of internet memes satirising the contest.[59] At Starmer's final session of Prime Minister's Questions, on 15 July 2026, Badenoch, the leader of the opposition, asked Starmer whether he agreed that the country deserved a televised debate between Farage and Binface. Starmer replied that his advice to everyone was to "put [their] vote in the Bin",[60][61] which was interpreted by The Daily Telegraph as an endorsement of Binface.[61]

In his manifesto published on 27 July, Binface announced 20 campaign pledges, including some targeting Farage, such as: "MPs who resign mid-parliament to be barred from the resulting by-election", and "I will not accept £5 million gifts from crypto billionaires (on Earth)". Regional policies included regenerating Walton Pier, and moving Parliament to the village of Weeley (a reference to "wheelie bins") while the Palace of Westminster is restored. He also pledged to represent the UK in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest, and that Clacton would host the 2028 contest if he won. Binface also noted that pledges from previous manifestos such as bringing back Ceefax, nationalising singer Adele, and moving the hand dryer in the gentlemen's toilets of the Crown and Treaty pub in Uxbridge, London, to a more sensible position, would carry over to his Clacton campaign.[55][62] In an interview with The i Paper, Binface said his first act would be to increase the size of the door aperture in the House of Commons, due to the fact that his outfit makes him eight feet tall and he would bang his head entering the chamber.[63] Under Parliamentary rules, he would not be permitted to wear his costume in the chamber.[64]

On the weekend before the vote, a Binface-supporter flew a light aircraft from Earls Colne Airfield, and spent half-an-hour making a flight path drawing of a bin off the coast of Essex near Clacton.[65] The media also photographed canvassers for Binface clad in dustbins distributing leaflets urging voters to "Clean up Clacton".[66][67] The Austin Powers vintage Union Jack Jaguar was called into service and toured Clacton all day in support of Binface.[68] The campaign illuminated Clacton on the eve of the contest with projected campaign slogans, manifesto pledges, and other visuals onto one of the "conveniently bin-shaped Martello towers" on the beachfront.[69]

Reclaim Party

On 7 July Laurence Fox, the leader of the Reclaim Party who lives in nearby West Mersea, announced he would be standing. Fox stated that he would "provide a voice on the 'right'" while also criticising the major parties for not standing a candidate against Farage, saying: "This is meant to be a democracy."[70][71][72] Fox has also said that Binface "literally is the establishment".[73]

Other candidates

  • William Clouston, the leader of the Social Democratic Party, announced on 17 July that he would stand.[74]
  • Abi Hookway, independent, whose policies include establishing a local dentist in Clacton and helping local businesses.[75] Hookway later pulled out of the election due to being sent multiple threats.[76]
  • The Official Monster Raving Loony Party, a satirical party, fielded three candidates; party leader Howling Laud Hope, Nick the Incredible Flying Brick, and Baron Von Thunderclap.[77][78] In response to Binface, one of the policies in their "manicfesto" was to "ban intergalatic [sic] interference in UK elections".[55][79]
  • James Ransley stood for the self-led Consensus Party.[80]
  • Kai Stephens was selected for the far-right British Democratic Party to contest the seat. He described his opponents as "subpar", including calling Binface a "failed leftist comedian" and Farage a "traitor who works in the interests of Zionism, capitalism, [and] globalism" and said he is "the only option on the paper that is serious, patriotic, and most importantly, nationalist".[81] On 8 August, Stephens and a group of BDP members staged a demonstration without permission at Clacton Pier, in which they attempted to hang a banner and light pyrotechnics, then verbally abused security staff after they were warned of the fire risks to the old pier.[82]
  • John Stevens, a former Conservative MEP and current deputy leader of Rejoin EU, a reaccessionist party.[83][84] Stevens previously stood for the Buckinghamshire Campaign for Democracy in Buckingham at the 2010 general election, finishing second behind Speaker of the House of Commons John Bercow and ahead of Farage.[85][86]

Public reaction

In response to Farage's resignation, the Daily Mirror's headline described the move as "desperate", but the Daily Express repeated Farage's narrative of "[letting] the people be the judges". The Daily Telegraph said that his gamble had turned to farce once the other major political parties decided to boycott the contest. The Times criticised Farage for trying to distract from legitimate questions about his financial dealings, and the i Paper described the tactics as "straight out of the Donald Trump playbook".[87] Politico reported on two local focus groups of voters who had supported Farage at the general election, who overwhelmingly agreed that the by-election was unnecessary and a farce. One group, consisting of nine voters, was prepared to stick with Farage (with one exception), but complained that the town had become a laughing stock with "an influx of idiots". Another group, consisting of disaffected Tory voters, had all soured on Farage and tended towards Binface.[68]

A nationwide poll of 1,000 British people by Ipsos in July 2026 found that 33% wanted Binface to win, as opposed to 21% for Farage.[88] Another poll by Survation found that 52% of people polled believed Farage triggered the by-election to detract attention from the financial investigations into him.[89][better source needed] The Ipsos poll found 74% of respondents wanted the standards committee investigation to continue. Furthermore, 54% of those polled said he should not have resigned his seat to force the by-election, seeing it as a tactic to avoid scrutiny and accountability.[88]

Analysis

Stephen Pollard, writing for The Spectator on 9 July, called the election a straight "two-way fight" between Farage and Binface, and speculated that the latter could win.[90] The political scientist Sir John Curtice, writing for The Telegraph, also on 9 July, said that Farage should "win comfortably" in Clacton, citing the strong majority in Clacton who voted to leave in the Brexit referendum.[91] Tom Harris proclaimed the election "a farce and a complete waste of time and money", adding that "it is a worrying indication that the man whom many still consider likely to become our next prime minister has an empty vacuum where a sense of judgment ought to be."[92] John Rentoul of The Independent said he assumed that Farage would win by an overwhelming margin on a low turnout,[93] but that the presence of Binface and other novelty candidates trivialised important questions about security following the killing of the Reform UK spokeswoman Ann Widdecombe.[94]

The Daily Mail published a commentary with the heading: "Farage is learning that when voters are shouting at you, it's bad. When they're laughing at you, it's over."[38] Conversely, Jawad Iqbal, writing in The Spectator said of Farage's decision to trigger the by-election: "It is a clever move – perhaps the only move he could make – which gives him a chance to retake control of the political narrative."[95] The academic Mark McGeoghegan said that he did not think Binface had any reasonable chance of winning, given that Clacton is the constituency in the UK most inclined to support Reform.[96]

According to Paul Whiteley, writing in The Conversation, Farage's situation was self-inflicted on multiple fronts, starting with a lack of financial transparency and breach of disclosure rules that has visibly damaged his standing, as the Reform electorate is a largely working-class, northern coalition likely to disapprove of a leader accepting large sums from an offshore billionaire. The deeper strategic error was assuming the contest would vindicate him and validate his outsider positioning; caught out by the mainstream parties' boycott, Farage instead faced what the Telegraph dubbed "joke parties" — Count Binface and the Monster Raving Loony Party. The by-election therefore risked undercutting the appearance of unstoppable momentum he wanted ahead of a general election. Finally, asked which parties were "on the side of the people", Reform (28%) trailed the Liberal Democrats (33%) and Greens (39%), with 36% seeing Reform as establishment-aligned, undermining the anti-establishment narrative that was his core strategic asset.[97]

In a video report, The Financial Express said that Count Binface had little to lose: "If he performs well, it reinforces his reputation as Britain's leading satirical candidate. If he performs poorly, that's exactly what most people expect". For Farage, conversely, the stakes are quite different: "This was his election. He called it, he framed it... A convincing victory would allow Farage to argue that his political message still resonates with voters. But if turnout disappoints, or if protest candidates perform unexpectedly well, critics are likely to argue that his anti-establishment narrative isn't quite as powerful as he claims. The symbolism matters almost as much as the result itself."[98] Lord Hayward, who specialises in polling, appeared to concur: "It could be a triple embarrassment... because Farage has to show that a large number of Clacton voters still support him." Already, with the absence of the major parties, how well candidates like Count Binface actually do will be an important indicator.[99]

It is estimated that the by-election cost the local council around £200,000-£250,000.[100][101]

Opinion polling

On 2 August, a constituency poll by Survation indicated that Farage was leading the polls with about 73%, with Binface polling at about 20%. The same poll found that in a two-way race between Farage and Binface, Farage would win 69% of the votes while Binface would get 31%.[102][103]

Result

Polling was held between 7:00 and 22:00 BST on 13 August 2026.[104] In the hours before the results were announced, addressing a group of Reform UK supporters, Farage said he would not attend the result as he had been told that there was an "organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result" and that he wanted to avoid being "demeaned and humiliated by nobodies".[105] A Reform UK spokesperson also said that a "credible threat" had been made against Farage.[106] Essex Police said that there was a robust policing presence around the count and that they had not advised any candidate not to attend.[107]

See also

  • 1986 Northern Ireland by-elections – similar by-elections where 15 of the 17 Northern Irish seats were vacated in protest of the Anglo-Irish Agreement and led to the re-election of all but one of the MPs;
  • Tatton in the 1997 general election – Martin Bell won a seat at the 1997 United Kingdom general election in the constituency of Tatton as an independent candidate after the major parties stood down to give him an unopposed run against sitting Conservative MP Neil Hamilton who was under investigation by the Parliamentary Standards Commissioner;
  • 2008 Haltemprice and Howden by-election – in which then-Shadow Home Secretary David Davis stood down to recontest the seat to spark debate on civil liberties. Similarly to Clacton, major parties stood aside, either due to supporting the campaign (the Liberal Democrats) or branding it a "political stunt" (Labour).
  • South Thanet – the constituency where Farage stood in the 2015 United Kingdom general election, in which one of the other candidates was comedian Al Murray in character as the Pub Landlord.

content_text: 2026 Clacton by-election ← 2024 13 August 2026 Next → Clacton constituencyRegistered79,785Turnout44.4% (14.3 pp) Candidate Nigel Farage Count Binface Party Reform Binface Popular vote 22,239 9,455 Percentage 63.3% 26.9% Swing 17.1 pp New MP before election Nigel Farage Reform Elected MP Nigel Farage Reform A by-election for the United Kingdom parliamentary constituency of Clacton was held on 13 August 2026, following the resignation of Nigel Farage, its member of Parliament. Farage, who is the leader of Reform UK, had represented Clacton since the 2024 general election. He announced on 7 July 2026 that he would vacate his seat to trigger a by-election and re-contest the constituency; his resignation was accepted the next day. The announcement came amid parliamentary scrutiny of Farage's personal finances, and allegations concerning undeclared gifts and support. The Labour Party, the Conservative Party, the Liberal Democrats, the Green Party and Restore Britain did not contest the by-election, leaving Count Binface, a novelty candidate, as the main challenger to Farage. Thirty-two other candidates were nominated, with the total of 34 breaking the record – previously set in 2008 – for the most candidates standing in any UK parliamentary election. The list included 18 independent candidates. Farage was re-elected with 22,239 votes (63.3% of those cast), followed by Binface with 9,455 (26.9%). The other 32 candidates received 3,417 (9.73%) of the vote, ranging from 7 to 492 (1.4%) votes per candidate. 20 candidates received 60 votes (0.17%) or less, including three different candidates from the Official Monster Raving Loony Party. Background Clacton Clacton is a coastal constituency in Essex, in the East of England. It is centred on Clacton-on-Sea and also includes other towns and villages in the Tendring area, including Frinton-on-Sea, Walton-on-the-Naze and Jaywick. According to 2021 census data, its residents are 96% ethnically White, and 44% of its residents belong to social grades A, B and C1.[1] The average gross household income is £33,147, below the average of £42,397 for Great Britain as a whole, and the home-ownership rate is 73%, against 64% nationally.[2] In the 2016 membership referendum, an estimated 73% of those who voted chose to leave the European Union.[3] The constituency is also known for being a target seat for right-wing populist parties;[4] the 2014 Clacton by-election was contested and won by Douglas Carswell, who had resigned as the member of Parliament (MP) for the constituency after defecting from the Conservative Party to the UK Independence Party (UKIP; at the time also led by Nigel Farage). The result made Carswell UKIP's first elected MP.[5] Investigation into Farage Farage's declaration that he was standing down followed reports of parliamentary investigations into his financial interests, his relationships with wealthy people, and other matters.[6][7][8] Specifically, the investigations involved: a payment of £5 million from the Thailand-based British businessman and cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne;[6] possible gifts in kind from George Cottrell, a British financier and political activist who was convicted of felony wire fraud in the United States in 2017;[9] allegations of lobbying the Bank of England regarding cryptocurrency;[10] declaration of several properties.[10] Farage's resignation interrupted the investigation process, though it would resume if he returned to Parliament.[11] Were Farage to be suspended from Parliament for more than 10 sitting days or 14 calendar days, it would trigger a recall petition, which if successful would result in a further by-election.[12] In addition to the parliamentary investigation, on the day of Farage's resignation as an MP it was reported that the £5 million payment from Harborne had also been reported to the United Kingdom's National Crime Agency by bankers under the anti-money laundering suspicious activity report scheme.[13][14] Other donations to Reform UK and other party leaders have also been flagged under the scheme.[15] Vacation of the seat On 7 July 2026 Farage announced that he would vacate his seat as MP for Clacton and stand again in the resulting by-election. He gave the investigations into him and his treatment by the press as reasons. Farage denied wrongdoing and said that he wanted voters in Clacton, rather than the press or parliamentary authorities, to decide whether he should continue as their MP.[16][17] On 8 July, Rachel Reeves, the chancellor of the exchequer, formalised his resignation by appointing him to the office of profit post of Steward and Bailiff of the Manor of Northstead to vacate his seat (as outright resignation from the Commons is not possible).[18] While objecting to his motives for resigning, she said "if he wants to spend the summer arguing with a bin, I won't stop him".[19][20] The writ to trigger the by-election was moved on 9 July,[21][22] and the date of 13 August was selected.[23] In the 21st century, there have been four instances where an incumbent MP has resigned and immediately stood in the ensuing by-election: David Davis at the 2008 Haltemprice and Howden by-election,[24] Douglas Carswell at the 2014 Clacton by-election,[25] Mark Reckless at the 2014 Rochester and Strood by-election[26] and Zac Goldsmith at the 2016 Richmond Park by-election.[27] All but Goldsmith retained their seats. Candidates The Statement of Persons Nominated was published after nominations closed on 17 July 2026.[23] Thirty-four candidates stood, breaking the record of 26 set at the 2008 Haltemprice and Howden by-election.[28][29] The large number of candidates resulted in the creation of the UK's largest ballot papers, measuring 90 cm (3 ft) in length, which cost four times more to print than regular ballots.[30] Ian Davidson, chief executive of Tendring District Council, told the BBC that the ballots, being longer than some of the tables used to count them on, meant that tables would have to be doubled for sorting ballots into batches before they could be verified and counted.[31] Declined to stand Shortly after Farage's announcement, the Labour Party, the Conservative Party, the Green Party, the Liberal Democrats and Restore Britain all stated they would not contest the by-election.[32][33] A Labour spokesperson called the situation "pathetic",[34] while Restore Britain leader Rupert Lowe said his party would not participate in "a Reform-sponsored media circus".[35] Green Party deputy leader Mothin Ali initially said (on 7 July) that the Greens stand in "every election",[36] but the party confirmed later that day that it would not nominate a candidate, describing the by-election as being designed to "serve Nigel Farage's personal political ambitions".[17] The Conservatives were reported to be targeting the seat in the next UK general election, but the party's leader, Kemi Badenoch, said that they would not stand in "Farage's fake by-election".[35] On 7 August, she wrote an open letter saying her party would participate in any second by-election.[37] The film journalist David Hughes, who stood as Lord Buckethead for the Official Monster Raving Loony Party at the 2019 general election in Uxbridge and South Ruislip, said many people had asked him to stand as Buckethead in Clacton, but that he was finished with the character and endorsed Count Binface instead.[38] Campaign Reform UK Nigel Farage Farage denied wrongdoing and described the contest as a "people versus the establishment" by-election.[17] Reform offered to pay for the costs of the by-election, estimated at around £200,000, but the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government stated that this would be illegal since elections are required to solely use public funds.[39][40] In an interview with the Daily Mail, Farage denied accusations that the by-election was a "farce", calling it a "real election with real people". He expressed surprise at the other parties' decision not to field candidates, which he described as "showing contempt" towards the electorate.[41] The Guardian reported on 9 July that Reform UK called on party activists to shift their focus from the Greater Manchester mayoral by-election on 30 July to support Farage in Clacton. Reform UK responded to the report by stating: "Our campaign plans for the Greater Manchester mayor by-election remain unchanged."[42] On 23 July, while Farage was campaigning in Clacton, a woman heckled Farage, shouting "wanker" as she drove past him, but while doing so crashed into the car in front of her while it was waiting at traffic lights. Farage later said: "That's what you might call instant karma!" in reference to the incident.[43][44] Count Binface Party Count Binface After the major parties declined to contest the election, the perennial novelty candidate Count Binface became the main contender to Farage in early media coverage, with The Independent reporting that Binface had become the focus of an anti-Farage tactical voting campaign.[45] Binface described himself as a "unity candidate".[46] In an interview with BBC Radio 4, Binface conceded that he would "probably not" win the election, but said that his job was "to celebrate and defend the wonders of British democracy".[47] He said his main appeal would be that he is not Farage.[48] Many mainstream politicians reacted to Binface's candidature with a mixture of amusement and approbation.[49] Badenoch, the Leader of the Opposition, said that if the by-election was a "people versus the establishment" that "Farage might be looking like the establishment and Count Binface maybe the people".[50] Keir Starmer, the prime minister, said he could not endorse Binface due to Labour Party rules.[51] Andy Burnham, who became prime minister the following month, posted a picture of himself shaking hands with Binface at a by-election.[52] He later said that Binface was "carrying the hopes of the nation".[53] Binface received a surge of support from activists after announcing his candidacy, raising more than £15,000 in donations in a day. He said he hoped to appeal to voters from all sides of the political spectrum and said he could even court the immigrant vote, given he was "the ultimate alien".[51] The green-energy industrialist Dale Vince, who has previously donated to Labour and the Green Party, offered to fund Binface's campaign.[54] Mr. C, former frontman of the psychedelic band the Shamen, re-recorded the band's 1992 number one single "Ebeneezer Goode" with lyrics about Binface, and filmed a music video.[55] Media personality Carol Vorderman urged Clacton's voters to support Binface.[56] Binface's campaign gained global media attention,[57][58] and has inspired a flood of internet memes satirising the contest.[59] At Starmer's final session of Prime Minister's Questions, on 15 July 2026, Badenoch, the leader of the opposition, asked Starmer whether he agreed that the country deserved a televised debate between Farage and Binface. Starmer replied that his advice to everyone was to "put [their] vote in the Bin",[60][61] which was interpreted by The Daily Telegraph as an endorsement of Binface.[61] In his manifesto published on 27 July, Binface announced 20 campaign pledges, including some targeting Farage, such as: "MPs who resign mid-parliament to be barred from the resulting by-election", and "I will not accept £5 million gifts from crypto billionaires (on Earth)". Regional policies included regenerating Walton Pier, and moving Parliament to the village of Weeley (a reference to "wheelie bins") while the Palace of Westminster is restored. He also pledged to represent the UK in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest, and that Clacton would host the 2028 contest if he won. Binface also noted that pledges from previous manifestos such as bringing back Ceefax, nationalising singer Adele, and moving the hand dryer in the gentlemen's toilets of the Crown and Treaty pub in Uxbridge, London, to a more sensible position, would carry over to his Clacton campaign.[55][62] In an interview with The i Paper, Binface said his first act would be to increase the size of the door aperture in the House of Commons, due to the fact that his outfit makes him eight feet tall and he would bang his head entering the chamber.[63] Under Parliamentary rules, he would not be permitted to wear his costume in the chamber.[64] On the weekend before the vote, a Binface-supporter flew a light aircraft from Earls Colne Airfield, and spent half-an-hour making a flight path drawing of a bin off the coast of Essex near Clacton.[65] The media also photographed canvassers for Binface clad in dustbins distributing leaflets urging voters to "Clean up Clacton".[66][67] The Austin Powers vintage Union Jack Jaguar was called into service and toured Clacton all day in support of Binface.[68] The campaign illuminated Clacton on the eve of the contest with projected campaign slogans, manifesto pledges, and other visuals onto one of the "conveniently bin-shaped Martello towers" on the beachfront.[69] Reclaim Party On 7 July Laurence Fox, the leader of the Reclaim Party who lives in nearby West Mersea, announced he would be standing. Fox stated that he would "provide a voice on the 'right'" while also criticising the major parties for not standing a candidate against Farage, saying: "This is meant to be a democracy."[70][71][72] Fox has also said that Binface "literally is the establishment".[73] Other candidates William Clouston, the leader of the Social Democratic Party, announced on 17 July that he would stand.[74] Abi Hookway, independent, whose policies include establishing a local dentist in Clacton and helping local businesses.[75] Hookway later pulled out of the election due to being sent multiple threats.[76] The Official Monster Raving Loony Party, a satirical party, fielded three candidates; party leader Howling Laud Hope, Nick the Incredible Flying Brick, and Baron Von Thunderclap.[77][78] In response to Binface, one of the policies in their "manicfesto" was to "ban intergalatic [sic] interference in UK elections".[55][79] James Ransley stood for the self-led Consensus Party.[80] Kai Stephens was selected for the far-right British Democratic Party to contest the seat. He described his opponents as "subpar", including calling Binface a "failed leftist comedian" and Farage a "traitor who works in the interests of Zionism, capitalism, [and] globalism" and said he is "the only option on the paper that is serious, patriotic, and most importantly, nationalist".[81] On 8 August, Stephens and a group of BDP members staged a demonstration without permission at Clacton Pier, in which they attempted to hang a banner and light pyrotechnics, then verbally abused security staff after they were warned of the fire risks to the old pier.[82] John Stevens, a former Conservative MEP and current deputy leader of Rejoin EU, a reaccessionist party.[83][84] Stevens previously stood for the Buckinghamshire Campaign for Democracy in Buckingham at the 2010 general election, finishing second behind Speaker of the House of Commons John Bercow and ahead of Farage.[85][86] Public reaction In response to Farage's resignation, the Daily Mirror's headline described the move as "desperate", but the Daily Express repeated Farage's narrative of "[letting] the people be the judges". The Daily Telegraph said that his gamble had turned to farce once the other major political parties decided to boycott the contest. The Times criticised Farage for trying to distract from legitimate questions about his financial dealings, and the i Paper described the tactics as "straight out of the Donald Trump playbook".[87] Politico reported on two local focus groups of voters who had supported Farage at the general election, who overwhelmingly agreed that the by-election was unnecessary and a farce. One group, consisting of nine voters, was prepared to stick with Farage (with one exception), but complained that the town had become a laughing stock with "an influx of idiots". Another group, consisting of disaffected Tory voters, had all soured on Farage and tended towards Binface.[68] A nationwide poll of 1,000 British people by Ipsos in July 2026 found that 33% wanted Binface to win, as opposed to 21% for Farage.[88] Another poll by Survation found that 52% of people polled believed Farage triggered the by-election to detract attention from the financial investigations into him.[89][better source needed] The Ipsos poll found 74% of respondents wanted the standards committee investigation to continue. Furthermore, 54% of those polled said he should not have resigned his seat to force the by-election, seeing it as a tactic to avoid scrutiny and accountability.[88] Analysis Stephen Pollard, writing for The Spectator on 9 July, called the election a straight "two-way fight" between Farage and Binface, and speculated that the latter could win.[90] The political scientist Sir John Curtice, writing for The Telegraph, also on 9 July, said that Farage should "win comfortably" in Clacton, citing the strong majority in Clacton who voted to leave in the Brexit referendum.[91] Tom Harris proclaimed the election "a farce and a complete waste of time and money", adding that "it is a worrying indication that the man whom many still consider likely to become our next prime minister has an empty vacuum where a sense of judgment ought to be."[92] John Rentoul of The Independent said he assumed that Farage would win by an overwhelming margin on a low turnout,[93] but that the presence of Binface and other novelty candidates trivialised important questions about security following the killing of the Reform UK spokeswoman Ann Widdecombe.[94] The Daily Mail published a commentary with the heading: "Farage is learning that when voters are shouting at you, it's bad. When they're laughing at you, it's over."[38] Conversely, Jawad Iqbal, writing in The Spectator said of Farage's decision to trigger the by-election: "It is a clever move – perhaps the only move he could make – which gives him a chance to retake control of the political narrative."[95] The academic Mark McGeoghegan said that he did not think Binface had any reasonable chance of winning, given that Clacton is the constituency in the UK most inclined to support Reform.[96] According to Paul Whiteley, writing in The Conversation, Farage's situation was self-inflicted on multiple fronts, starting with a lack of financial transparency and breach of disclosure rules that has visibly damaged his standing, as the Reform electorate is a largely working-class, northern coalition likely to disapprove of a leader accepting large sums from an offshore billionaire. The deeper strategic error was assuming the contest would vindicate him and validate his outsider positioning; caught out by the mainstream parties' boycott, Farage instead faced what the Telegraph dubbed "joke parties" — Count Binface and the Monster Raving Loony Party. The by-election therefore risked undercutting the appearance of unstoppable momentum he wanted ahead of a general election. Finally, asked which parties were "on the side of the people", Reform (28%) trailed the Liberal Democrats (33%) and Greens (39%), with 36% seeing Reform as establishment-aligned, undermining the anti-establishment narrative that was his core strategic asset.[97] In a video report, The Financial Express said that Count Binface had little to lose: "If he performs well, it reinforces his reputation as Britain's leading satirical candidate. If he performs poorly, that's exactly what most people expect". For Farage, conversely, the stakes are quite different: "This was his election. He called it, he framed it... A convincing victory would allow Farage to argue that his political message still resonates with voters. But if turnout disappoints, or if protest candidates perform unexpectedly well, critics are likely to argue that his anti-establishment narrative isn't quite as powerful as he claims. The symbolism matters almost as much as the result itself."[98] Lord Hayward, who specialises in polling, appeared to concur: "It could be a triple embarrassment... because Farage has to show that a large number of Clacton voters still support him." Already, with the absence of the major parties, how well candidates like Count Binface actually do will be an important indicator.[99] It is estimated that the by-election cost the local council around £200,000-£250,000.[100][101] Opinion polling On 2 August, a constituency poll by Survation indicated that Farage was leading the polls with about 73%, with Binface polling at about 20%. The same poll found that in a two-way race between Farage and Binface, Farage would win 69% of the votes while Binface would get 31%.[102][103] Date(s)conducted Pollster Samplesize Reform Binface Reclaim Other Lead 13 Aug 2026 2026 by-election 35,111 63.3% 26.9% 1.0% 8.8% 36.4 16–24 Jul 2026 Survation[102][103] 503 73% 20% 2% 5% 53 4 Jul 2024 2024 general election 45,958 46.2% — — 53.8%[a] 18.3[b] Result Polling was held between 7:00 and 22:00 BST on 13 August 2026.[104] In the hours before the results were announced, addressing a group of Reform UK supporters, Farage said he would not attend the result as he had been told that there was an "organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result" and that he wanted to avoid being "demeaned and humiliated by nobodies".[105] A Reform UK spokesperson also said that a "credible threat" had been made against Farage.[106] Essex Police said that there was a robust policing presence around the count and that they had not advised any candidate not to attend.[107] Previous result See also 1986 Northern Ireland by-elections – similar by-elections where 15 of the 17 Northern Irish seats were vacated in protest of the Anglo-Irish Agreement and led to the re-election of all but one of the MPs; Tatton in the 1997 general election – Martin Bell won a seat at the 1997 United Kingdom general election in the constituency of Tatton as an independent candidate after the major parties stood down to give him an unopposed run against sitting Conservative MP Neil Hamilton who was under investigation by the Parliamentary Standards Commissioner; 2008 Haltemprice and Howden by-election – in which then-Shadow Home Secretary David Davis stood down to recontest the seat to spark debate on civil liberties. Similarly to Clacton, major parties stood aside, either due to supporting the campaign (the Liberal Democrats) or branding it a "political stunt" (Labour). blocks.html_en: A by-election for the United Kingdom parliamentary constituency of Clacton was held on 13 August 2026, following the resignation of Nigel Farage, its member of Parliament. Farage, who is the leader of Reform UK, had represented Clacton since the 2024 general election. He announced on 7 July 2026 that he would vacate his seat to trigger a by-election and re-contest the constituency; his resignation was accepted the next day. The announcement came amid parliamentary scrutiny of Farage's personal finances, and allegations concerning undeclared gifts and support.

blocks.html_en: The Labour Party, the Conservative Party, the Liberal Democrats, the Green Party and Restore Britain did not contest the by-election, leaving Count Binface, a novelty candidate, as the main challenger to Farage. Thirty-two other candidates were nominated, with the total of 34 breaking the record – previously set in 2008 – for the most candidates standing in any UK parliamentary election. The list included 18 independent candidates.

blocks.html_en: Clacton is a coastal constituency in Essex, in the East of England. It is centred on Clacton-on-Sea and also includes other towns and villages in the Tendring area, including Frinton-on-Sea, Walton-on-the-Naze and Jaywick. According to 2021 census data, its residents are 96% ethnically White, and 44% of its residents belong to social grades A, B and C1.[1] The average gross household income is £33,147, below the average of £42,397 for Great Britain as a whole, and the home-ownership rate is 73%, against 64% nationally.[2] In the 2016 membership referendum, an estimated 73% of those who voted chose to leave the European Union.[3] The constituency is also known for being a target seat for right-wing populist parties;[4] the 2014 Clacton by-election was contested and won by Douglas Carswell, who had resigned as the member of Parliament (MP) for the constituency after defecting from the Conservative Party to the UK Independence Party (UKIP; at the time also led by Nigel Farage). The result made Carswell UKIP's first elected MP.[5]

blocks.html_en: On 7 July 2026 Farage announced that he would vacate his seat as MP for Clacton and stand again in the resulting by-election. Farage denied wrongdoing and said that he wanted voters in Clacton, rather than the press or parliamentary authorities, to decide whether he should continue as their MP.[16][17] On 8 July, Rachel Reeves, the chancellor of the exchequer, formalised his resignation by appointing him to the office of profit post of Steward and Bailiff of the Manor of Northstead to vacate his seat (as outright resignation from the Commons is not possible).[18] While objecting to his motives for resigning, she said "if he wants to spend the summer arguing with a bin, I won't stop him".[19][20] The writ to trigger the by-election was moved on 9 July,[21][22] and the date of 13 August was selected.[23] In the 21st century, there have been four instances where an incumbent MP has resigned and immediately stood in the ensuing by-election: David Davis at the 2008 Haltemprice and Howden by-election,[24] Douglas Carswell at the 2014 Clacton by-election,[25] Mark Reckless at the 2014 Rochester and Strood by-election[26] and Zac Goldsmith at the 2016 Richmond Park by-election.[27] All but Goldsmith retained their seats.

blocks.html_en: In response to Farage's resignation, the Daily Mirror's headline described the move as "desperate", but the Daily Express repeated Farage's narrative of "[letting] the people be the judges". blocks.html_en: According to Paul Whiteley, writing in The Conversation, Farage's situation was self-inflicted on multiple fronts, starting with a lack of financial transparency and breach of disclosure rules that has visibly damaged his standing, as the Reform electorate is a largely working-class, northern coalition likely to disapprove of a leader accepting large sums from an offshore billionaire. The deeper strategic error was assuming the contest would vindicate him and validate his outsider positioning; caught out by the mainstream parties' boycott, Farage instead faced what the Telegraph dubbed "joke parties" — Count Binface and the Monster Raving Loony Party. The by-election therefore risked undercutting the appearance of unstoppable momentum he wanted ahead of a general election. Finally, asked which parties were "on the side of the people", Reform (28%) trailed the Liberal Democrats (33%) and Greens (39%), with 36% seeing Reform as establishment-aligned, undermining the anti-establishment narrative that was his core strategic asset.[97]

2026 Clacton by-election

克拉克顿选区
挂号的79,785
结果发现44.4% (14.3 pp)
候选人 Nigel Farage 计数 Binface 政党改革 Binface 普选票 22,239 9,455 百分比 63.3% 26.9% 摇摆 17.1 pp 新
选举前议员 奈杰尔·法拉奇·改革 当选议员 奈杰尔·法拉奇·改革

英国议会克拉克顿选区在议会议员奈杰尔·法拉奇辞职后于 2026 年 8 月 13 日举行了补选。 法拉奇是英国改革党的领导人，自 2024 年大选以来一直代表克拉克顿。 他于2026年7月7日宣布腾出议席引发补选，重新竞选选区；第二天他的辞呈就被接受了。 这一消息是在议会对法拉奇个人财务进行审查以及有关未申报的礼物和支持的指控之际发布的。

工党、保守党、自由民主党、绿党和复兴英国都没有参加补选，使得新奇候选人宾法斯伯爵成为法拉奇的主要挑战者。 另外 32 名候选人获得提名，其中 34 名候选人打破了 2008 年创下的英国议会选举中候选人最多的纪录。 该名单包括 18 名独立候选人。

Farage 以 22,239 票（占总投票数的 63.3%）再次当选，Binface 以 9,455 票（26.9%）紧随其后。 其他 32 名候选人获得 3,417 票（9.73%）选票，每位候选人获得 7 票至 492 票（1.4%）不等。 20 名候选人获得 60 票（0.17%）或更少，其中包括来自官方 Monster Raving Loony 党的三名不同候选人。

背景

克拉克顿

克拉克顿是英格兰东部埃塞克斯郡的一个沿海选区。 它以滨海克拉克顿为中心，还包括 Tendring 地区的其他城镇和村庄，包括滨海弗林顿、内兹沃尔顿和杰威克。 根据2021年人口普查数据，其居民96%为白人，44%的居民属于社会等级A、B和C1。 [1]平均家庭总收入为 33,147 英镑，低于整个英国 42,397 英镑的平均水平，住房拥有率为 73%，而全国为 64%。 [2]在2016年的脱欧公投中，估计有73%的投票者选择离开欧盟。[3]该选区还因成为右翼民粹主义政党的目标席位而闻名；[4] 2014 年克拉克顿补选由道格拉斯·卡斯韦尔 (Douglas Carswell) 竞选并获胜，他在从保守党叛逃到英国独立党 (UKIP；当时也由奈杰尔·法拉奇 (Nigel Farage) 领导）后辞去了该选区议会议员 (MP) 的职务。 结果使卡斯韦尔成为英国独立党第一位当选议员。[5]

对法拉奇的调查

法拉奇宣布辞职之前，有报道称议会正在调查他的经济利益、与富人的关系以及其他事务。[6][7][8]具体而言，调查涉及：来自泰国的英国商人和加密货币投资者 Christopher Harbourne 支付的 500 万英镑；[6] 英国金融家和政治活动家 George Cottrell 可能提供的实物礼物，他于 2017 年在美国被判犯有电汇欺诈重罪；[9] 就加密货币问题游说英格兰银行的指控；[10] 申报多项财产。 [10]

法拉奇的辞职中断了调查过程，但如果他回到议会，调查就会恢复。 [11]如果法拉奇被议会停职超过 10 天或 14 个日历日，就会引发罢免请愿，如果成功，将导致进一步补选。 [12]除了议会调查外，据报道，在法拉奇辞去议员职务当天，银行家还根据反洗钱可疑活动报告计划，向英国国家犯罪局报告了Harborne支付的500万英镑款项。 [13][14]该计划还标记了向改革英国和其他政党领导人提供的其他捐款。 [15]

座位休假

2026 年 7 月 7 日，法拉奇宣布他将辞去克拉克顿议员席位，并在随后的补选中再次参选。 他以对他的调查和媒体对他的待遇作为理由。 法拉奇否认有不当行为，并表示他希望克拉克顿的选民，而不是媒体或议会当局来决定他是否应该继续担任议员。[16][17] 7 月 8 日，财政大臣雷切尔·里夫斯 (Rachel Reeves) 正式辞职，任命他担任诺斯泰德庄园管家兼法警的职务，以腾出席位（因为从下议院彻底辞职是不可能的）。 [18]在反对他辞职的动机时，她说“如果他想整个夏天和垃圾箱争论，我不会阻止他”。 [19][20]触发补选的令状于7月9日提出，[21][22]，日期选定为8月13日。[23]在 21 世纪，有过四次现任议员辞职并立即参加随后的补选的情况：2008 年 Haltemprice 和 Howden 补选中的 David Davis、2014 年 Clacton 补选中的 Douglas Carswell、[25] 2014 年 Rochester 和 Strood 补选中的 Mark Reckless[26] 以及 2014 年 Rochester 和 Strood 补选中的 Zac Goldsmith。 2016年里士满公园补选。[27]除戈德史密斯外，所有人都保留了席位。

候选人

提名人声明于 2026 年 7 月 17 日提名结束后发布。[23] 34 名候选人参选，打破了 2008 年 Haltemprice 和 Howden 补选时创下的 26 名候选人的纪录。 [28][29]大量候选人催生了英国最大的选票，长度为 90 厘米（3 英尺），其印刷成本是普通选票的四倍。 [30] Tendring 区议会首席执行官伊恩·戴维森 (Ian Davidson) 告诉 BBC，选票比一些用于计票的桌子还要长，这意味着必须将桌子加倍，才能将选票分批分拣，然后才能进行验证和计票。 [31]

拒绝起立

法拉奇宣布这一消息后不久，工党、保守党、绿党、自由民主党和复兴英国党均表示不会参加补选。 [32][33]工党发言人称这种情况“可悲”，[34]而复兴英国领导人鲁珀特·洛表示，他的政党不会参加“改革赞助的媒体马戏团”。[35]绿党副领袖 Mothin Ali 最初（7 月 7 日）表示绿党参加“每次选举”，[36] 但该党当天晚些时候证实不会提名候选人，并将补选描述为“服务于奈杰尔·法拉奇的个人政治野心”。 [17]

据报道，保守党的目标是在下届英国大选中获得席位，但该党领袖凯米·巴德诺克表示，他们不会参加“法拉奇的假补选”。 [35] 8月7日，她写了一封公开信，表示她的政党将参加任何第二次补选。 [37]电影记者大卫·休斯 (David Hughes) 在 2019 年乌克斯布里奇 (Uxbridge) 和南莱斯利普 (South Ruislip) 大选中代表官方怪兽狂欢党 (Monster Raving Loony Party) 担任巴克海德勋爵 (Lord Buckethead)，他表示很多人曾要求他在克拉克顿 (Clacton) 担任巴克海德勋爵 (Lord Buckethead)，但他已经厌倦了这个角色，转而支持宾法斯伯爵 (Count Binface)。 [38]

活动

改革英国

法拉奇否认有不当行为，并将这次竞选描述为“人民与建制派”的补选。 [17]改革提议支付补选费用，估计约为 20 万英镑，但住房、社区和地方政府部表示，这是非法的，因为选举必须仅使用公共资金。 [39][40]法拉奇在接受《每日邮报》采访时否认了补选是一场“闹剧”的指控，称这是“真正的人民的真正选举”。 他对其他政党不派候选人的决定表示惊讶，他称这是对选民的“蔑视”。 [41]

英国《卫报》7月9日报道，改革英国呼吁党内活动人士将注意力从7月30日的大曼彻斯特市长补选转移到支持克拉克顿的法拉奇。 英国改革组织回应该报道称：“我们大曼彻斯特市长补选的竞选计划保持不变。”[42] 7月23日，法拉奇在克拉克顿竞选时，一名妇女在开车经过法拉奇身边时大喊“混蛋”，质问法拉奇，但在这样做时撞上了她前面正在等红绿灯的汽车。 法拉奇后来说：“这就是你所说的即时业力！” 提及该事件。[43][44]

计数 Binface 派对

在主要政党拒绝参加选举后，常年新奇的候选人宾法斯伯爵成为早期媒体报道中法拉奇的主要竞争者，《独立报》报道称宾法斯伯爵已成为反法拉奇战术投票活动的焦点。 [45] Binface 将自己描述为“团结候选人”。 [46]在接受 BBC 广播 4 台采访时，宾法斯承认他“可能不会”赢得选举，但表示他的工作是“庆祝和捍卫英国民主的奇迹”。 [47]他说他的主要吸引力是他不是法拉奇。[48]

许多主流政治家对宾法斯的候选资格的反应既有趣又赞许。 [49]反对党领袖巴德诺克表示，如果补选是一场“人民与建制派”的较量，那么“法拉奇可能看起来像建制派，而宾法斯伯爵则可能是人民”。 [50]总理凯尔·斯塔默 (Keir Starmer) 表示，由于工党的规定，他不能支持 Binface。 [51]下个月成为总理的安迪·伯纳姆（Andy Burnham）发布了一张自己在补选中与宾法斯握手的照片。 [52]他后来说Binface“承载着国家的希望”。 [53]

Binface 在宣布参选后获得了活动人士的大力支持，一天之内筹集了超过 15,000 英镑的捐款。 他说他希望吸引来自政治光谱各方面的选民，并表示他甚至可以争取移民选票，因为他是“终极外星人”。 [51]此前曾向工党和绿党捐款的绿色能源实业家戴尔·文斯 (Dale Vince) 主动提出为 Binface 的竞选活动提供资金。 [54]迷幻乐队 The Shamen 的前主唱 Mr. C 重新录制了该乐队 1992 年的冠军单曲《Ebeneezer Goode》，歌词涉及 Binface，并拍摄了音乐视频。 [55]媒体名人 Carol Vorderman 敦促 Clacton 的选民支持 Binface。 [56] Binface 的竞选活动引起了全球媒体的关注，[57][58] 并引发了大量讽刺这场比赛的网络表情包。[59] 2026 年 7 月 15 日，在斯塔默举行的最后一次总理提问会议上，反对党领袖巴德诺克询问斯塔默是否同意法拉奇和宾法斯在该国进行电视辩论。 Starmer 回答说，他对每个人的建议是“将[他们的]选票投进垃圾桶”，[60][61]这被《每日电讯报》解读为对 Binface 的认可。[61]

在 7 月 27 日发表的宣言中，Binface 宣布了 20 项竞选承诺，其中包括一些针对 Farage 的承诺，例如：“在议会中期辞职的议员将被禁止参加由此产生的补选”，以及“我不会接受来自（地球上）加密货币亿万富翁的 500 万英镑礼物”。 地区政策包括重建沃尔顿码头，以及将议会迁至威利村（指“带轮垃圾箱”），同时修复威斯敏斯特宫。 他还承诺代表英国参加 2027 年欧洲歌唱大赛，如果获胜，克拉克顿将主办 2028 年比赛。 Binface 还指出，之前宣言中的承诺，例如带回 Ceefax、将歌手阿黛尔国有化，以及将伦敦乌克斯布里奇皇冠和条约酒吧绅士卫生间的干手器移至更明智的位置，将延续到他的克拉克顿竞选活动中。 [55][62]在接受《i Paper》采访时，宾法斯表示，他的第一个行动是增加下议院门洞的尺寸，因为他的服装使他有八英尺高，进入议事厅时他会用头撞。 [63]根据议会规定，他不被允许在会议厅穿着他的服装。 [64]

投票前的周末，一名 Binface 支持者从伯爵科恩机场驾驶一架轻型飞机，花了半个小时在克拉克顿附近的埃塞克斯海岸绘制了一个垃圾箱的飞行路线。 [65]媒体还拍到 Binface 的游说者穿着垃圾箱分发传单，敦促选民“清理克拉克顿”。 [66][67]奥斯汀鲍尔斯老式英国国旗捷豹被投入使用并全天巡游克拉克顿以支持宾法斯。 [68]该活动在比赛前夕将竞选口号、宣言承诺和其他视觉效果投射到海滨的一栋“方便的垃圾箱形状的马泰洛塔”上，照亮了克拉克顿。 [69]

回收党

7 月 7 日，居住在西默西附近的光复党领袖劳伦斯·福克斯 (Laurence Fox) 宣布他将参选。 福克斯表示，他将“为‘右派’发出声音”，同时批评主要政党没有派出候选人来对抗法拉奇，他说：“这意味着民主。”[70][71][72]福克斯还表示，Binface“实际上就是建制派”。[73]

公众反应

针对法拉奇的辞职，《每日镜报》的头条新闻将这一举动描述为“绝望”，但《每日快报》则重复了法拉奇“让人民来评判”的说法。 《每日电讯报》称，一旦其他主要政党决定抵制这次竞选，他的赌博就变成了闹剧。 《泰晤士报》批评法拉奇试图转移人们对有关其财务交易的合法问题的注意力，《i Paper》将这种策略描述为“直接出自唐纳德·特朗普的剧本”。 [87] 《政治报》报道了在大选中支持法拉奇的两个当地选民焦点小组的情况，他们绝大多数认为补选是不必要的，是一场闹剧。 一个由九名选民组成的团体准备支持法拉奇（除了一个例外），但抱怨该镇因“白痴涌入”而成为笑柄。 另一组由心怀不满的保守党选民组成，他们都对法拉奇感到不满，并倾向于宾法斯。 [68]

益普索 (Ipsos) 于 2026 年 7 月对 1,000 名英国人进行的一项全国性民意调查发现，33% 的人希望 Binface 获胜，而 21% 的人希望 Farage 获胜。 [88] Survation 的另一项民意调查发现，52% 的受访者认为 Farage 引发补选是为了分散对他的财务调查的注意力。[89][需要更好的消息来源]Ipsos 民意调查发现，74% 的受访者希望标准委员会调查继续进行。 此外，54% 的受访者表示，他不应该辞去席位来强制进行补选，认为这是避免审查和问责的一种策略。 [88]

分析

7 月 9 日，斯蒂芬·波拉德 (Stephen Pollard) 为《旁观者》撰稿，称此次选举是法拉奇和宾法斯之间的直接“双向斗争”，并推测后者可能获胜。 [90]政治学家约翰·柯蒂斯爵士也在 7 月 9 日为《电讯报》撰稿，表示法拉奇应该在克拉克顿“轻松获胜”，并援引了克拉克顿绝大多数在英国脱欧公投中投票支持脱欧的人的说法。 [91]汤姆·哈里斯 (Tom Harris) 宣称这次选举“一场闹剧，完全浪费时间和金钱”，并补充道，“这是一个令人担忧的迹象，许多人仍然认为有可能成为我们下一任首相的人在应该有判断力的地方却出现了真空。”[92] 《独立报》的约翰·伦图尔 (John Rentoul) 表示，他认为法拉奇将以压倒性优势在低投票率下获胜，[93] 但宾法斯和其他新奇候选人的出现忽视了改革被扼杀后有关安全的重要问题。英国发言人安·维德科姆。[94]

《每日邮报》发表了一篇评论，标题是：“法拉奇了解到，当选民对你大喊大叫时，这是很糟糕的。 当他们嘲笑你的时候，一切就结束了。”[38] 相反，贾瓦德·伊克巴尔在《旁观者》杂志上撰文谈到法拉奇触发补选的决定时说道：“这是一个聪明的举动——也许是他能做出的唯一举动——这让他有机会重新控制政治叙事。”[95] 学者马克·麦克盖根 (Mark McGeoghegan) 表示，鉴于克拉克顿是最佳候选人，他认为宾法斯没有任何合理的获胜机会。英国最倾向于支持改革的选区。[96]

保罗·怀特利在《对话》中写道，法拉奇的处境在多个方面都是自找的，首先是缺乏财务透明度和违反披露规则，这明显损害了他的地位，因为改革派选民主要是工薪阶层，北方联盟可能不赞成领导人接受海外亿万富翁的大笔资金。 更深层次的战略错误是假设这场比赛会证明他的正确性并验证他的局外人定位；由于受到主流政党的抵制，法拉奇反而面临着《每日电讯报》所称的“笑话派对”——宾法斯伯爵和怪物疯狂疯子党。 因此，补选可能会削弱他在大选前所希望的不可阻挡的势头。 最后，当被问及哪些政党“站在人民一边”时，改革党（28%）落后于自由民主党（33%）和绿党（39%），36%的人认为改革党与建制派保持一致，破坏了作为其核心战略资产的反建制叙事。 [97]

《金融快报》在视频报道中表示，宾法斯伯爵没什么可失去的：“如果他表现出色，就会巩固他作为英国领先讽刺候选人的声誉。 如果他表现不佳，那正是大多数人所期望的”。 相反，对于法拉奇来说，赌注却截然不同：“这是他的选举。 他称呼它，他陷害它…… 令人信服的胜利将使法拉奇能够辩称，他的政治信息仍然能引起选民的共鸣。 但如果投票率令人失望，或者抗议候选人的表现出乎意料地好，批评者可能会认为他的反建制叙事并不像他声称的那么强大。 象征意义几乎和结果本身一样重要。”[98] 专门从事民意调查的海沃德勋爵似乎也同意：“这可能是三重尴尬...... 因为法拉奇必须证明大量的克拉克顿选民仍然支持他。” 由于主要政党缺席，像宾法斯伯爵这样的候选人实际上表现如何将成为一个重要指标。 [99]

据估计，补选花费了地方议会约20万至25万英镑。[100][101]

结果

投票于 2026 年 8 月 13 日英国夏令时间 7:00 至 22:00 之间举行。[104]在结果公布前的几个小时，法拉奇向一群英国改革支持者发表讲话，表示他不会出席结果，因为他被告知存在“一场有组织的活动来扰乱和贬低结果”，并且他希望避免“被无名之辈贬低和羞辱”。 [105]英国改革派发言人还表示，法拉奇受到了“可信的威胁”。 [106]埃塞克斯警方表示，计票地点周围有强大的警力，他们没有建议任何候选人不要参加。[107]
